```{r, include = FALSE}
# Not evaluated: it needs a Databricks workspace and a token.
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", eval = FALSE)
```

Databricks workspaces speak Spark Connect, so zuspark can query them
directly: no `databricks-connect`, no Python and no JVM. You need the
workspace's URL, a personal access token, and one extra header that tells
Databricks which compute to run on. This article shows serverless compute,
which is all that Databricks Free Edition offers and which needs no cluster
to be started.

```{r setup}
library(zuspark)
```

## Get a workspace URL and a token

The workspace URL is the start of the address in your browser while you
are in the workspace, up to the domain, such as
`https://dbc-1a2b3c4d-5e6f.cloud.databricks.com`. Leave out the path and
the `?o=` part.

To create a token, click your avatar in the top right corner, then
**Settings**, **Developer**, and **Manage** next to **Access tokens**.
Generate a new token and copy it: Databricks shows it only once.

Keep both out of your scripts. One way is to put them in `~/.Renviron`,
which R reads at start-up:

```sh
DATABRICKS_HOST=https://dbc-1a2b3c4d-5e6f.cloud.databricks.com
DATABRICKS_TOKEN=dapi...
```

## Connect to serverless compute

Spark Connect on Databricks runs over TLS on port 443. Serverless compute
also needs an `x-databricks-session-id` header that carries the session
id; without it, the server answers *"Invalid compute mode headers"*.
Choose the session id yourself, and give it to zuspark both as the session
id and as that header:

```{r}
host <- sub("^https://", "", Sys.getenv("DATABRICKS_HOST"))
session <- as.character(zuid::uuid(version = 4))

con <- spark_connect(
  sprintf("sc://%s:443/;use_ssl=true", host),
  token = Sys.getenv("DATABRICKS_TOKEN"),
  session_id = session,
  headers = c("x-databricks-session-id" = session)
)
spark_version(con)
```

`spark_version()` reports the Spark version of the Databricks runtime
behind the session. Serverless compute starts by itself when the session
connects, and the first query can take a few seconds while it does.

## Run SQL

From here on, a Databricks session works like any other Spark Connect
session:

```{r}
q <- spark_sql(con, "SELECT id, id * 2 AS twice FROM range(5)")
spark_schema(q)
spark_collect(q)
```

Tables in Unity Catalog are queried by their three-part names, such as
those of the `samples` catalog, where a workspace has it:

```{r}
spark_collect(spark_sql(con, "
  SELECT pickup_zip, count(*) AS trips
  FROM samples.nyctaxi.trips
  GROUP BY pickup_zip
  ORDER BY trips DESC
  LIMIT 5
"))
```

Spark's errors arrive with their error class and SQLSTATE, and
`spark_error_details()` asks the workspace for the rest:

```{r}
err <- tryCatch(spark_sql(con, "SELECT * FROM no_such_table"), error = identity)
err$error_class
err$sql_state
spark_error_details(err)[[1]]$message
```

## Disconnect

`spark_disconnect()` releases the session on the workspace, so its
serverless compute can stop:

```{r}
spark_disconnect(con)
```

## Classic compute

A workspace with clusters (not Free Edition) takes the cluster's id in an
`x-databricks-cluster-id` header instead of the session header. The cluster
must be running. This path has not been tested with zuspark yet:

```{r}
con <- spark_connect(
  sprintf("sc://%s:443/;use_ssl=true", host),
  token = Sys.getenv("DATABRICKS_TOKEN"),
  headers = c("x-databricks-cluster-id" = "0123-456789-abcdefgh")
)
```
